entries.reason: a promise is not a value this engine has, so this is the port's own ES5 promise - the one +[JSValue valueWithNewPromiseInContext:fromExecutor:] builds - and the same constructor, the same executor and the same promise object, not a second promise (charon_js_deferred_promise, CharonJSPromise.m)
entries.effect: answers a promise and the two functions that settle it, both functions of their own. A resolve reaches a reaction the promise was given, on the next run loop turn rather than as the call returns, which is the difference +[JSValue valueWithNewPromiseInContext:fromExecutor:] already carries: the release with a native promise drains its microtask queue as the outermost call into script returns, and this queue has no leave of its own to run at when a C client makes the call itself. A rejection through the C API leaves its reaction unrun on this engine and on the host's own one alike, measured in the same run and asserted on neither. NULL with the exception left where the caller reads it when the promise could not be made

entries.reason: a context's name is the label a Web Inspector lists the context under, and this port carries no Web Inspector: there is no protocol here that could be attached, so nothing would ever read the name. It is carried inert rather than absent because the answer this port can give is the answer a release with no inspector gives, and a client weak-linking the symbol is answered rather than left to crash
entries.effect: the name is not kept and the call says so in the log the first time an application reaches it. It is not bridged to -[JSContext setName:], which keeps a name in its own wrapper with no other reader either: the wrapper registry holds weakly by design, so a store a C client could reach would have to outlive the wrapper and die with the context, and the only such store the release has, a JSWeakObjectMap, holds JavaScript values rather than a name
